name: California Mission Colonial

revival_periods.note: Driven by railroad tourism, Charles Fletcher Lummis's Landmarks Club and the Ramona myth; the revival abstracted the shaped parapet gable and the arcade and discarded the quadrangle.
The richer successor, launched by Goodhue's Panama-California Exposition, drawing on Mexican and Andalusian sources the missions themselves never had.

regions: coastal California from San Diego to Sonoma
geography.hearth: the twenty-one Franciscan missions founded between San Diego (1769) and Sonoma (1823), plus their associated presidios and pueblos

lineage.note: Founded and supplied from Mexico. The Franciscans came from the College of San Fernando in Mexico City; the master masons, the tile, the bells and the plans came up from New Spain, and San Luis Rey's plan was drawn from a Mexican model.

description.short: The Franciscan mission quadrangle of Alta California: adobe walls under low half-round clay tile, arcaded corredors on square piers, and all the province's ornament spent on one church front.
description.long:
The California missions were not built as architecture. They were built as self-sufficient agricultural and manufacturing complexes with a church attached, by an indigenous labour force under a coercive system, at a rate of roughly one every two years for sixty-five years, under the direction of friars who were not architects and who had access to almost no skilled masons. Understanding that production system explains everything about how they look.

The organizing figure is the quadrangle: a closed square, one hundred and fifty to three hundred feet on a side, formed by ranges of single-loaded rooms one span deep — workshops, granaries, weaving rooms, the friars' quarters, the monjerío — with the church occupying one corner and its facade turned outward to the approach. The court is the only public space and the only safe one. The rooms face into it through an arcaded corredor ten to fourteen feet deep, and that corredor is the circulation system of the entire complex: there are no internal corridors anywhere, and one crosses the open air to move from any room to any other.

The arcade itself is the type's most legible element and the most consistently misread. These are square masonry piers, not columns — usually two and a half to four feet wide, carrying semicircular arches whose clear opening runs one and a half to two and a half times the pier width. There is no order, no base, no capital, and often no impost moulding. That squatness is not naivety; it is what unreinforced adobe and rubble can do. Above sits a low roof, three to five in twelve, of half-round clay tile — thatch until fires and the arrival of tile-makers around 1790 — with an eave of twelve to twenty inches and no gutter.

Ornament was rationed to the point of severity. Domestic and workshop ranges are entirely plain: whitewashed lime plaster over adobe, undulating, with no mouldings. Everything the mission could afford in the way of carving and colour went onto one surface — the church portada — and to the campanario, a pierced bell wall or a detached tower. Santa Barbara's church, built 1815–20 by the master mason José Antonio Ramírez, went further than any of the others: engaged Ionic columns and a neoclassical temple front flanked by twin campaniles, worked in local sandstone with famously crude mortar joints, a Vitruvian composition executed by people with no Vitruvian training. The tension in that facade — high classical ambition, frankly rough execution — is the most honest thing about the whole tradition.

To walk a mission corredor at four in the afternoon is to understand why the twentieth century could not stop imitating it: a hundred and fifty feet of deep shade, a warm rough wall on one side, an open sunlit court on the other, and the arch rhythm slow enough to walk in time with.

defining_characteristics: A closed or three-sided quadrangle 150–300 ft on a side, formed by ranges of single-loaded rooms one span deep, with the church at one corner
Arcaded corredor 10–14 ft deep on square masonry piers carrying semicircular arches, serving as all circulation
Adobe or rubble walls, 24–36 in in the ranges and 3–5 ft at the church, lime-plastered and whitewashed
Low-pitched roof, 3:12 to 5:12, of half-round clay tile (teja) after c. 1790, with a 12–20 in eave and no gutter
Campanario — a pierced bell wall — or a detached or engaged bell tower at the church
Ornament confined to the church portada and the campanario; all other surfaces plain whitewashed plaster
Buttresses or thickened piers wherever wall height exceeds roughly eight times wall thickness
diagnostic_tells: Square piers, not columns, under semicircular arches, with no capitals and often no imposts
The arcade faces the court and stops at the corners; the outer face of the quadrangle is largely blind
Tile roof with a shallow pitch and a very short eave — the roof reads as a lid, not as a shelter
Whitewashed plaster that visibly undulates over the adobe beneath it
One decorated surface in the entire complex, and it is the church door

distinguished_from.difference: The 1890s revival takes the shaped or curvilinear parapet gable — a feature of only a few mission facades — and makes it the signature, applies quatrefoil windows, builds arcades of thin piers on wood frame or brick with stucco, and abandons the quadrangle entirely. It also builds two and three storeys, which the adobe original could not.

Both build in adobe. New Mexico roofs flat on vigas behind a parapet with canales and uses no arch, no arcade and no tile; California pitches a tile roof at 3:12–5:12 and organizes everything around an arcaded court.

Monterey is the secular, Anglo-inflected California adobe of the 1830s and 40s: two storeys, a cantilevered wooden balcony, a shingle hip roof and double-hung sash. Mission work is single-storey, ecclesiastical or institutional, tile-roofed and arcaded.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The arcade bay — pier width to arch opening — sets the rhythm of the whole complex; wall thickness is set by height, and room depth by the available roof timber.
typical_ratios: Pier width 2 ft 6 in – 4 ft; arch clear opening 1.5 to 2.5 times the pier width
Arch springing 7–9 ft above the corredor floor; corredor depth 10–14 ft
Wall thickness 24–36 in in the ranges, 36–60 in at the church; height not more than 8× thickness without buttressing
Quadrangle 150–300 ft square; church nave 25–35 ft clear, 100–180 ft long
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: A long, slow, uninterrupted arcade of identical bays, typically ten to twenty of them, with no accent, no centre and no termination other than the corner of the court.

massing_affinities.note: Missions whose fourth range was never completed, or asistencias.
The single arcaded range of an outlying rancho or asistencia.
The individual room of a range, which is the repeated unit of the whole thing.

constraints.statement: Arcade geometry: square masonry piers 2 ft 6 in – 4 ft wide carrying semicircular arches whose clear opening is 1.5 to 2.5 times the pier width. Slender piers or columns with capitals convert the arcade into a revival and are structurally impossible in adobe.

test.note: 2ft6in-4ft converted to inches. The arch-opening-to-pier-width ratio (1.5-2.5x) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 under half-round clay tile, with an eave projection of 12–20 in and no gutter. Pitches above 6:12 are foreign to the tradition.

test.note: Eave projection (12-20in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Adobe or rubble wall not less than 24 in in the ranges; where wall height exceeds eight times thickness, external buttresses are required at not more than 15 ft on centre.

test.note: The conditional buttress-spacing clause stays prose.

constraints.statement: Corredor depth not less than 10 ft. Below that it stops functioning as circulation and shade and becomes a covered walk.
Carved or moulded ornament permitted only at the church portada and the campanario. Distributing ornament across the ranges converts the complex into Spanish Colonial Revival.

exemplars.name: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia
exemplars.note: Founded 1798; the surviving cruciform church of 1811–15 and the largest of the mission quadrangles, sometimes called the King of the Missions.

exemplars.name: Mission Santa Barbara church
exemplars.note: Built 1815–20 by master mason José Antonio Ramírez after the 1812 earthquake destroyed the adobe predecessor. Twin campaniles flanking a temple front with engaged Ionic columns, in rough-hewn stone with crude joints; second tower 1831–33, both rebuilt after the 1925 earthquake, facade reconstructed 1950–53.

exemplars.name: Serra Chapel, Mission San Juan Capistrano
exemplars.note: The oldest standing building in California and the only surviving church in which Junípero Serra is known to have said Mass; the adjoining Great Stone Church of 1806 collapsed in the 1812 earthquake and stands as a ruin.

exemplars.name: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel
exemplars.note: Church completed 1805 with buttressed side walls and a detached campanario of six bells — the pierced bell wall in its clearest form.

sources: Rexford Newcomb, The Old Mission Churches and Historic Houses of California (1925)
Kurt Baer, Architecture of the California Missions (1958)
Harold Kirker, California's Architectural Frontier: Style and Tradition in the Nineteenth Century (1960)
David Gebhard and Robert Winter, An Architectural Guidebook to Los Angeles (rev. eds.)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: Bound primary, and this node contributed the pack's most useful disagreement. Its own defining_characteristics say 'buttresses or thickened piers wherever wall height exceeds roughly eight times wall thickness', where the New Mexico code family says ten. The pack records that as a BAND of 8-10 rather than averaging it away, because both are right for their own case: the code figure assumes a continuous reinforced bond beam tying the wall head and the mission builders had none, and answered the difference with the buttresses this record names. The 24-36 in ranges are two adobes; the 3-5 ft church wall is three. vignola-ionic stays optional and unaffected -- it governs the church front's applied order, which is a different building from the ranges behind it.

Applies to the range rooms only (workshops, granaries, cells -- 15-20 ft deep, single-loaded, per this node's own record), not to the church nave, which the pack's measured band (11-18 ft) does not reach and which this node records separately (25-35 ft clear). Within that scope the fit is real: room depth here is capped by the same beam-span physics room-vernacular reconstructs from Anglo-American evidence, even though the beam is a different species and the wall behind it is adobe or rubble rather than framed. As with the parent spanish-colonial-american node, no pack in this corpus governs the mass wall itself or the arcade [SUPERSEDED 25 Aug 2026: both are now governed -- `adobe-module` holds the mass wall and `facade-arcade` holds the arcade, and the c01 numbers quoted below are two of the nine records that pack's central ratio rests on] -- see this node's own arcade geometry constraint (c01), which states real numbers (pier 2 ft 6 in - 4 ft, arch clear opening 1.5-2.5x pier) that exist in this node's own text because no proportion pack here derives them. SUPERSEDED 25 Aug 2026: the mass-wall/adobe module this sentence asked for is `adobe-module`, bound primary on this node. The arcade system is still missing and is still in WP-4.1's candidate list -- adobe-module carries the post-and-zapata portal and not the arched range.

Bound only for the named exception this node itself records, not for the type: Mission Santa Barbara's church front (built 1815-20 by master mason Jose Antonio Ramirez) carries engaged Ionic columns and a neoclassical temple pediment in local sandstone -- 'a Vitruvian composition executed by people with no Vitruvian training,' in this node's own words. Vignola rather than a named overlay (Gibbs, Palladio, Chambers, Benjamin) because there is no documentary evidence connecting a specific pattern book to Ramirez's work, so the base order is the honest choice rather than inventing a source. This entry governs a single church facade among dozens of mission buildings and should not be read as describing the type.

The node whose binding note asked for this pack. Its `room-vernacular` entry says in terms that 'an arcade/portal system' is missing from the corpus, alongside the mass-wall gap that `adobe-module` closed. This is that pack. The record supplies the springing height rule outright -- 'arch springing 7-9 ft above the corredor floor' -- and the corredor depth at 10-14 ft, and it is one of the four records that say the arcade is the circulation: 'arcaded corredor 10-14 ft deep on square masonry piers carrying semicircular arches, serving as all circulation'.

'Carved or moulded ornament permitted only at the church portada and the campanario. Distributing ornament across the ranges converts the complex into Spanish Colonial Revival.' The same ration as `spanish-colonial-american`, stated for a complex rather than a building, and with the same consequence named. Bound behind `adobe-module`, which owns the walls, and `facade-arcade`, which owns the corredor: this pack owns only the two places where the whitewash stops. Worth reading the pack's cost conflict against this node in particular, since the missions were built by an unskilled coerced labour force under friars who were not architects, and concentrating the entire ornament budget at one panel is what made any ornament possible at all.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes say what it is: the horseshoe arch, the impost block, the alfiz and the geometric setting-out — "kind is `order-system` because this IS the system of support and springing" — and its module block names the impost assembly as "the diagnostic member of the whole system", whose loss "turns the arcade into a classical one wearing a horseshoe". This node's arcade is the negative of that record on both counts at once: square masonry piers, semicircular arches, no capitals, often no imposts. The one rule reaching the node is the alfiz at `window_surround_masonry`, an ornamental frame around an opening, in a type whose ranges are "entirely plain: whitewashed lime plaster over adobe, undulating, with no mouldings" and whose one decorated surface is the church door — and that surface is already dimensioned here by `facade-portada` and `vignola-ionic`, a neoclassical temple front, not a Hispano-Islamic one. It arrives from `spanish-plateresque` at cascade depth 5 with no direct lineage edge.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes say it is Palladio's Doric as an OVERLAY ON VIGNOLA, and that its three load-bearing claims are the 30-minute module, the Attic base ('if a building is Palladian this base is on the drawing') and the diminution tabulated by column height — an authority claim about which pattern book dimensions a column. This node's record answers that authority question explicitly and in the opposite direction: its one classical facade, Santa Barbara's church front, is bound to the BASE order precisely because no named overlay can be evidenced, and Palladio is named in the list refused. Behind that single exception the type has no column at all — description.long says of the arcade 'There is no order, no base, no capital, and often no impost moulding', and the first diagnostic tell repeats it. So the node contradicts the pack twice over: no order in the ranges, and at the one place an order exists, a refusal of this overlay by name.
